components.description: Probability laws and their weak convergence
components.source_items: p. 116: F_n => F at continuity points of F; X_n => X ('converge weakly or converge in distribution') through the distribution functions P(X_n <= x). The routed text matches this and adds that no common probability space is needed.

components.description: The source inverse convention and its plateau endpoints
components.source_items: p. 118: Y_n(x) = sup{y : F_n(y) < x} on ((0,1), Borel, Lebesgue); the F^{-1} notation; a_x = sup{y : F(y) < x}, b_x = inf{y : F(y) > x}. All of these are present, and Q_F is identified with the source's F^{-1}.

components.description: CDF uniqueness and measurable inverse realization
components.source_items: p. 116: right continuity plus countably many discontinuities (Exercise 1.2.3) identify the limit. p. 118: the Theorem 1.2.2 premise that Y_n has distribution F_n, and F(y) < x for y < F^{-1}(x), F(z) > x for z > F^{-1}(x). Proofs are written for countable jumps, dense continuity points, uniqueness of a proper weak limit, finiteness and order of a and b, Q_F = inf{F >= u}, the exact ray identity, measurability, and the CDF of Q_F. Uniqueness of the law cites thm:p15-cdf-laws (handbook/parts/p15/measurable-probability.tex 427, on the route).

components.description: Durrett 3.2.8: almost-sure common-space realization
components.source_items: pp. 118-119: the statement; the countable exceptional set (disjoint intervals (a_x,b_x), each holding a distinct rational); proof steps (a) liminf >= and (b) limsup <=. All are written. Disjointness is proved through b(u) <= a(v) for u < v. A boundary line notes that only the marginal laws are preserved. The source sentence 'Theorem 3.2.8 allows us to immediately generalize some of our earlier results' names no specific result; the generalizations it refers to (Exercises 3.2.4-3.2.5) are routed through C024 to thm:p15-criteria-weak-integration.

components.description: Durrett 3.2.9: bounded continuous test functions
components.source_items: p. 119: the introductory claim that Theorem 3.2.9 'illustrates the usefulness of Theorem 3.2.8 and gives an equivalent definition of weak convergence that makes sense in any topological space'; the statement of Theorem 3.2.9; the coupling and bounded-convergence direction; the converse through the ramps g_{x,eps}, with the limsup and liminf bounds. The theorem and both proof directions are present on the route. The topological-space claim is absent on the route and appears only in the unrouted owned files.
components.gap: Supply on the route the source's p. 119 claim that the bounded-continuous characterization gives an equivalent definition of weak convergence that makes sense in any topological space. The routed entry (parts 90-110, annex 101-141) states and proves only the real-line equivalence. The claim, with the definition, its well-definedness and its agreement with def:p15-weak-law-convergence on the line, is written in full with proofs in the owned files (parts w02c-p15-004 6-12 and 69-165; annex w02c-p15-004 6-157). Those files are not input in handbook/parts/p15.tex or handbook/annex/p15.tex, so the only remaining action is routing.

components.description: Durrett 3.2.10: the exact discontinuity-set hypothesis
components.source_items: p. 120: both conclusions (g(X_n) => g(X), and E g(X_n) -> E g(X) for bounded g); the Remark that D_g is always Borel (Exercise 1.3.6); the proof through D_{f o g} contained in D_g, bounded convergence and Theorem 3.2.9; the easier second conclusion. All are written. D_g is proved Borel by the closed-set route and by the source's upper/lower-envelope route, on the real line as the theorem requires.

components.description: Interior, closure and continuity sets

evidence.label: annex:p15.weak-portmanteau (use of the boundary, ray boundary {x})

components.source_items: p. 121: closure, interior and the boundary (closure minus interior), as used in (ii)&(iii) => (iv), and P(X in boundary of A) = 0. All are present.

components.description: Durrett 3.2.11: the portmanteau equivalences

evidence.label: thm:p15-weak-convergence-boundaries item 1 (single instance of the Remark)

components.source_items: pp. 120-121: equivalence of (i)-(iv); the Remark ('consider the special case in which P(X_n = x_n) = 1 ... if x_n in G and x_n -> x in the boundary of G, then P(X_n in G) = 1 for all n but P(X in G) = 0. Letting K = G^c gives an example for (iii)'); the proofs of (i)=>(ii) by Fatou, (ii)<=>(iii), (ii)&(iii)=>(iv), and (iv)=>(i) with A = (-infinity,x]. The theorem and its proof cycle are complete on the route. The Remark appears on the route only as one instance; its general form is only in the unrouted owned files.
components.gap: Supply on the route the source's p. 120 Remark in the generality it states: for every open G and every point-mass sequence with x_n in G and x_n -> x in the boundary of G, P(X_n in G) = 1 for all n while P(X in G) = 0, giving strict inequality in (ii); and K = G^c gives the example for (iii). The route carries only the instance x_n = 1/n, G = (0,infinity), K = (-infinity,0] (parts 439-442; annex 851-860), a narrowed variant. The general remark with proof is written in the owned files (parts w02c-p15-004 167-233; annex w02c-p15-004 159-238). Those files are not input on the route, so the only remaining action is routing.

components.description: The source's possibly defective CDF limit
components.source_items: p. 121 Remark: the limit may not be a distribution function; the example a+b+c = 1, F_n = a1(x>=n) + b1(x>=-n) + cG -> b + cG with endpoint limits b and b+c = 1-a; mass a escapes to +infinity and mass b to -infinity; the name vague convergence and the notation =>_v. All are present, with proofs.

components.description: Durrett 3.2.12: the full real-line selection construction
components.source_items: pp. 121-122: the statement; the diagonal argument over an enumeration of the rationals; F(x) = inf{G(q) : q rational, q > x} and its right continuity; convergence at continuity points through rationals r1 < r2 < x < s. All steps are written, with the scalar selection premise proved by bisection and the remaining finite measure constructed.

components.description: The source tightness convention
components.source_items: p. 122: for all eps > 0 there is M_eps with limsup_n 1 - F_n(M_eps) + F_n(-M_eps) <= eps. This is stated exactly. The added uniform formulation is proved equivalent.

components.description: Durrett 3.2.13: exactly when all selected limits are proper
components.source_items: p. 122: the question of when no mass is lost; Theorem 3.2.13 in both directions, with the continuity points r < -M, s > M, and the non-tight subsequence n(k) with H_{n(k)}(k) >= eps followed by a further selection. Both directions are written, together with the additional equivalences.

components.description: Durrett 3.2.14: a coercive moment bound
components.source_items: p. 123: phi >= 0 with phi(x) -> infinity as |x| -> infinity and C = sup_n integral phi dF_n < infinity imply tightness; proof bound 1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M) <= C / inf_{|x|>=M} phi(x). Coercivity is stated in an equivalent form. The bound C/L, with phi >= L on |x| >= M, contains the source's bound (take L = inf_{|x|>=M} phi when it is finite and positive), and the tail event (-infinity,-M] u (M,infinity) is contained in {|x| >= M}.

components.description: The Levy and Ky Fan metrics
components.source_items: p. 124: Exercise 3.2.6 rho(F,G) = inf{eps : F(x-eps) - eps <= G(x) <= F(x+eps) + eps for all x}; Exercise 3.2.7 alpha(X,Y) = inf{eps >= 0 : P(|X-Y| > eps) <= eps}. Both are defined exactly, together with the metric notion and almost-sure identification.

components.description: The source metric premises and the probability bridge
components.source_items: p. 123: 'Exercises 3.2.6 and 3.2.7 define metrics for convergence in distribution'. p. 124: Exercise 3.2.6 (rho is a metric; rho(F_n,F) -> 0 iff F_n => F); Exercise 3.2.7 (alpha(X,Y) = eps implies rho(F,G) <= eps); Exercise 3.2.12 (convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution; X_n => c implies convergence in probability). All are proved with written steps: symmetry, triangle inequality, identity of indiscernibles, both directions of the rho characterization by a continuity-point partition, the alpha metric with attained infimum, alpha against convergence in probability, rho <= alpha, and the constant converse through the closed-set portmanteau bound.

components.description: Durrett 3.2.15 and the unique-limit method
components.source_items: p. 123: 'The fact that convergence in distribution comes from a metric immediately implies' Theorem 3.2.15. The source's metric argument is written from the proved premises, and a direct CDF proof is added. The source's forward note that the result is proved again at the end of Theorem 3.3.17 belongs to Section 3.3 and adds no obligation here.

components.description: The source total-variation convention
components.source_items: p. 117: ||mu_n - mu|| = sup_B |mu_n(B) - mu(B)|. The supremum-over-events convention is stated. The half-L1 identity is proved in annex 560-566.

components.description: Scheffe's theorem in Section 3.2

evidence.label: thm:p15-weak-convergence-boundaries item 1 (point mass at 1/n, total variation one)

components.source_items: p. 117: probability densities f_n -> f pointwise; |integral_B f_n - integral_B f| <= integral |f_n - f| = 2 integral (f - f_n)^+ -> 0 by dominated convergence, using f_n >= 0 with integral one; total variation -> 0, 'a conclusion stronger than weak convergence (Take B = (-infinity, x])'; the example of the point mass at 1/n with mu_n => mu and ||mu_n - mu|| = 1. All are present. The source's pointwise Lebesgue-density case is declared a special case of the routed almost-everywhere, general-measure statement.

components.description: The product limit and central-binomial premise
components.source_items: Premises invoked on pp. 116-118, checked on pp. 113-115: Lemma 3.1.1 (c_j -> 0, a_j -> infinity, a_j c_j -> lambda imply (1+c_j)^{a_j} -> e^lambda); Exercise 3.1.1 (the array version under max |c_{j,n}| -> 0, sum -> lambda and bounded absolute sums); Theorem 3.1.2 at k = 0 (P(S_{2n} = 0) ~ (pi n)^{-1/2}). The scalar and array versions are proved with the log remainder bound. C_n sqrt(pi n) -> 1 is proved through the cosine integrals I_n = pi C_n and dominated convergence, against the established Gaussian integral (thm:p15-normal-normalization, handbook/parts/p15/convolution-gamma-normal.tex 301, on the route).

components.description: Durrett Example 3.2.1, with its needed limit proved
components.source_items: p. 116: P(S_n/sqrt n <= y) -> the standard normal integral, via Theorem 3.1.3 (p. 115, including the odd-index step S_{2n+1} = S_{2n} +/- 1). Written steps cover: the binomial local masses and their ratio product; the uniform local estimate on bounded scaled intervals; the Riemann sum with endpoint control; the tail through Chebyshev; and odd N through the sandwich with moving thresholds. The limit holds at every y, as the source's later comment on Examples 3.2.1-3.2.2 says.

components.description: Durrett Examples 3.2.2--3.2.5
components.source_items: pp. 116-117: Example 3.2.2 (Glivenko-Cantelli, a.e. omega, all y, possible discontinuities), proved from thm:p15-glivenko-cantelli (handbook/parts/p15/strong-law-applications.tex 164, on the route). 'In the last two examples convergence occurred for all y ... the next example shows why we restrict our attention to continuity points'. Example 3.2.3 (F(x - 1/n) -> F(x-), convergence only at continuity points). Example 3.2.4 (P(X_p >= n) = (1-p)^{n-1}; P(pX_p > x) -> e^{-x}; exponential limit). Example 3.2.5: the product formula; the birthday reading under equally likely birthdays (annex 752-785: 'For birthdays', uniform model, no nonuniform birth frequencies); P(T_N/N^{1/2} > x) -> exp(-x^2/2) through Exercise 3.1.1; the N = 365, n = 22 approximation e^{-0.6630} = 0.515 (stated as e^{-484/730} = 0.5152960451); the true value 0.524 (0.5243046923). The source's '2% smaller' comparison is not restated as a percentage, but both compared values are given at higher precision, so the comparison is present in substance.

components.description: Durrett Example 3.2.6 and Lemma 3.2.7
components.source_items: pp. 117-118: the (n+1)th largest of 2n+1 uniform points; the density (2n+1) binom(2n,n) x^n (1-x)^n by index counting, with the eps-window alternative replaced by an exact Borel-set integral via Tonelli; Y_n = 2(V_{n+1} - 1/2) sqrt(2n) by change of variables (Exercise 1.2.5 premise = thm:p15-affine-lebesgue, handbook/parts/p15/convolution-gamma-normal.tex 64, on the route); the factorized f_{Y_n}; the first factor as P(S_{2n} = 0) (annex 643); the limit through Theorem 3.1.2 and Lemma 3.1.1 (premises proved in C019); the density reading of P(Y_n = y); weak convergence by Scheffe. All are written.

components.description: What weak convergence does not preserve
components.source_items: The source boundaries are: p. 117 (point mass at 1/n, total variation one); p. 120 (portmanteau strictness, here as an instance: the general Remark is judged under C008); p. 121 (the a,b,c escaping-mass example). The handbook adds countermodels for 1_{0}, a fair sign against convergence in probability, the unbounded test x, and normalization in Scheffe. All six items are stated and proved.

Every cited label is defined in a file on the route: thm:p15-stirling-with-remainder, thm:p15-stirling-de-moivre-laplace, thm:p15-characteristic-inversion-uniqueness, thm:p15-characteristic-continuity-theorem, thm:p15-characteristic-second-moment, sec:p15-characteristic-function-criteria-and-moments, thm:p15-criteria-weak-integration, sec:p15-central-limit-theorems, thm:p15-nda-characterization, thm:p15-nda-normalizer-construction, thm:p15-nda-gk-truncated-mean, thm:p15-nda-gk-cutoff-route, sec:p15-weak-convergence-exercises. The boundary does not mention the p. 119 claim or the general p. 120 Remark; those are judged under C005 and C008.
